title.full: Canadian Energy Outlook, 3rd edition – Pathways for a net-zero Canada: Horizon 2060

publisher.full: Institut de l'énergie Trottier, Polytechnique Montréal

description: Normative least-cost Canadian pathway to net zero by 2050, with -40% vs 2005 by 2030 (NATEM).
pathwayDescription: Published in 2024 by the Institut de l’énergie Trottier (Polytechnique Montréal) as part of the third Canadian Energy Outlook, Pathways for a net-zero Canada – Horizon 2060, the study explores, province by province, the least-cost pathways for transforming Canada’s energy system and reaching net-zero emissions. The Net-zero by 2050 scenario (NZ50) is a normative pathway that finds the least-cost way for Canada to reach net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, with an interim cut of 40% below 2005 levels by 2030. It covers all sectors and gases, but excludes land use and international aviation and shipping. The publication does not state an associated temperature outcome. Getting there requires electrifying most energy services, which more than doubles electricity generation to about 1,280 TWh by 2050, with wind and small modular reactors as the main new sources. Crude oil production falls by 93%. About 130 Mt of CO2 removals a year by 2050, from bioenergy with carbon capture, biochar and direct air capture, offset the remaining emissions from agriculture, industrial processes and transport. For comparison, REF cuts emissions only about 25% below 2005 levels by 2050.

coreDrivers.policies: The pathway implements the same policy drivers as in Reference Scenario: Clean Electricity Regulations, carbon prices, Clean Fuel Regulations, ZEV mandate, clean-technology/hydrogen/CCUS tax credits. In NZ50 they are no longer the binding drivers: the report notes the carbon price path to 2030 is insufficient for the 2030 target, so the emissions constraint does most of the work.
coreDrivers.emissionsTargets: National net-zero constraint on total CO2e in 2050 plus a 40% cut vs 2005 by 2030, mirroring the two legislated federal targets; reductions are allocated across provinces at least cost, so some provinces go net-negative while others stay positive.
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: Least-cost optimisation under the net-zero constraint selects the mix: SMRs (34.6 GW by 2050) and wind (97 GW) as main new generation under central SMR cost projections, blue and biomass-CCS hydrogen over electrolysis, and DAC only from the 2040s because of very high cost. The marginal abatement cost of the last tonne is $880/t CO2e versus $1,100/t in CEO 2021, reflecting lower technology costs. NZ50PS tests pessimistic SMR costs.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: Same GDP and Statistics Canada medium population growth as REF drive service demand, but NZ50 uses CER Global Net-Zero export prices, lowering export demand: crude oil production falls 93% by 2050 versus growth in REF. This export-price assumption is a key differentiator from REF alongside the emissions constraint. .
coreDrivers.otherDrivers: A finite biomass resource caps bioenergy at about 1,000 PJ and, as net zero approaches, diverts it from combustion to negative-emission uses (BECCS power and hydrogen, biochar from syngas), which drives the post-2040 mix of the power, buildings and hydrogen sectors.

dependencies.dependency_description: NZ50 needs power generation to double to 4,604 PJ by 2050 and power to go net-negative (-16.6 Mt) through BECCS; current measures are 'far from sufficient' and the report calls for coherent provincial and federal plans to 2050, subsector roadmaps and a national plan for interprovincial interconnections. Without such a strategy the 2040s acceleration is unlikely.

Building capacity a decade ahead of demand and doubling generation require regulators and utilities to accept anticipatory investment and smart two-way grids; current readiness varies widely, permitting and investment barriers raise costs above European levels, and peak-capacity limits already block electrification in Quebec. These rules set the pace of NZ50's post-2040 ramp.

NZ50's doubled generation and SMR-led baseload rest on cost projections the report says need care: the first SMR has yet to be built to confirm costs, and capture costs may be underestimated. The marginal abatement cost reaches $880/t CO2e for the last tonne, though under $80/t for the 2030 target. Electrification yields net system savings, but without tariff reform gains are unevenly shared, risking opposition.

NZ50 builds 34.6 GW of SMRs (22% of 2050 generation) and 97 GW of wind; SMR futures are 'clouded' by social acceptance and construction delays, and the report lists social acceptance among barriers making net-zero dependent on rapid strategies.

Near-total electrification of heating (electricity 82.9% of building energy by 2050) and transport sharpens winter peaks; the report notes peak-management strategies are not modelled but needed to avoid over-building. Consumer acceptance of demand-response therefore affects the capacity NZ50 requires.

Doubling generation needs commensurate transmission, distribution upgrades for new consumption profiles, storage of 18.8 GW (9.0 GW batteries, 7.6 GW pumped hydro) and winter-peak capacity, built ahead of demand. Analysis is annual/seasonal without hourly dispatch, so flexibility needs are approximated. Grid growth is already a constraint as Hydro-Québec already refuses full heating electrification for lack of peak capacity and a slower growth would constraint electrification.

NZ50 depends on SMRs reaching commercial scale (1,004 PJ, 22% of 2050 generation, costs decrease by 23% from now to 2050), BECCS power for negative emissions, and grid batteries (9.0 GW). SMRs have not reached commercial scale anywhere, and the NZ50PS sibling shows the mix shifts substantially if SMR costs disappoint.

BECCS power competes for a finite biomass supply (bioenergy capped near 1,000 PJ), and grid and generation build-out faces supply-chain constraints for key components; both limit how fast NZ50's power mix can be delivered.

A build-out 'equivalent or larger than' 1960-1990 needs workers for construction and operation of grids, competing with hundreds of thousands needed for retrofits and heat pumps; the report says ambitious objectives are unlikely at this pace without aggressive workforce strategies.

Steel emissions fall 87% by 2050 (to 1.8 Mt) only under the national net-zero constraint; the report says industry needs tailored roadmaps, including for process emissions, developed as soon as possible, otherwise Canadian industrial decarbonisation depends on regulations elsewhere.

byMetric.scopeLimitations: National power-generation emissions in MtCO2e, Scope 1, including negative emissions from BECCS power. Fuel extraction for power sits in 'Oil, gas and coal production' and is not separable. 2021 baseline differs slightly across Explorer scenario files (75.1-77.1 Mt).

granularity: High-carbon assets lifetime face early retirement policy
byMetric.scopeLimitations: Retirement is regulation-driven via the CER, which excludes Nunavut, Northwest Territories, Yukon and remote communities; existing units are modelled individually. No asset-lifetime table is published.

Installed capacity, GW. Storage figure covers centralized batteries, decentralized batteries, pumped hydro, flywheel and hydrogen storage; one combined series in the report figure, broken down by type in the Explorer export - 2050 total 18.8 GW (9.0 centralized battery, 2.3 decentralized battery, 7.6 pumped hydro). Decentralized (rooftop) PV and batteries reported separately in Explorer. No captive industrial series.

Derived: 'Electricity production' emissions ('Figure 4.8') / generation excl. storage ('Figure 2.5'). Scope 1 CO2e. BECCS power is netted in, so intensity is negative in net-zero pathways by 2050. Explorer 'Electricity' emissions also include a 'Heat' line, excluded here. Distributed (rooftop) PV included in generation.

Electricity generation in PJ. Figure lists a small 'Storage' output line (1-35 PJ), excluded here. Explorer separates centralized and decentralized (rooftop) PV. On-grid and distributed generation are both included; no captive industrial series. Provincial generation by source exists for all 13 jurisdictions in the Chapter 5 dataset.

LIMITATION - period totals: values are 10-year period totals, each covering the decade ending in its label year (2040 = 2031-2040); divide by 10 for an annual average (e.g. NZ50 2041-2050 $509bn -> ~$51bn/yr). Reviewer interpretation, not documented in the export; discounting basis unknown. Aggregate electricity-sector investment in $ (Power10=3), plus 'Fix operation cost'. No technology split, no 2021 value.

Investment cost for 2022, 2030, 2050 and one fixed O&M value per technology; no variable O&M or fuel costs shown. Two SMR rows: optimistic (REF, NZ50) and pessimistic (NZ50PS). Storage split into 4h/8h utility batteries, decentralized batteries, pumped hydro and compressed air (peak and seasonal). No transmission costs.
Derived: technology generation / total generation excl. storage. Not reported directly as shares. Provincial generation technology mix also exists for all 13 jurisdictions in the Chapter 5 dataset.

Iron and steel = combustion ('Figure 4.6') + process ('Figure 4.7') emissions, MtCO2e, Scope 1. Ironmaking and steelmaking not separated; no power-related (Scope 2) emissions; any steel CCS is not attributed (industrial CCS reported only economy-wide, 'Figure 4.9').
Only two steel options are costed: hydrogen direct iron reduction and CCS capture (as a capex multiplier); no costs for conventional BF-BOF, EAF or scrap routes. Values constant 2022-2050.
